properties.name: Green Faction Headquarters
properties.one_line: The Greens ran their Circus Maximus chariot team from a headquarters here, marked by a dedication stone that named the spot the statio Prasina. A medieval church later built on the site kept the memory alive as San Lorenzo in Prasino.
properties.notes: The inscription CIL VI 10058 was found in situ near the present church of San Lorenzo in Damaso, whose medieval alternate name, S. Laurentii in Prasino, preserves the faction's color. Of the four factions, the Greens are the only one with a securely located statio in the city center rather than just the general stable district near the Circus Flaminius.
sources: Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stabula IIII Factionum
CIL VI 10058
Digital Augustan Rome, s.v. Stabula Factionum

properties.name: Blue Faction Headquarters
properties.one_line: Excavators found possible traces of the Blues' faction headquarters beneath the later Palazzo Farnese, in the stable district south of the Campus Martius where all four racing factions kept their operations near the Circus Flaminius.
properties.notes: Remains attributed to the factio Veneta were reported beneath Palazzo Farnese and the neighboring Palazzo Regis, but the identification rests on find circumstances rather than an in-situ dedication like the Greens' statio, so the exact footprint of the Blues' complex is less certain.
sources: Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stabula IIII Factionum
Digital Augustan Rome, s.v. Stabula Factionum

properties.name: Red Faction Headquarters
properties.one_line: The Reds, one of the two oldest racing factions along with the Whites, kept a headquarters somewhere in the cluster of stables south of the Campus Martius near the Circus Flaminius and the Trigarium training ground.
properties.notes: No excavated building has been tied to the Reds specifically. This point marks the general stabula factionum district near the Trigarium and the Circus Flaminius rather than a confirmed findspot; treat it as a district-level approximation only.
sources: Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stabula IIII Factionum
John H. Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986)

properties.name: White Faction Headquarters
properties.one_line: The Whites, paired with the Reds as the oldest of the racing factions, based their Rome operation in the same stable district near the Circus Flaminius, though its exact footprint has never been excavated.
properties.notes: No excavated building has been tied to the Whites specifically. This point marks the general stabula factionum district near the Trigarium and the Circus Flaminius rather than a confirmed findspot; treat it as a district-level approximation only.
sources: Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stabula IIII Factionum
John H. Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986)

properties.name: Castra Praetoria
properties.one_line: The praetorian prefect Sejanus built this walled camp in 23 CE to concentrate the emperor's nine Praetorian cohorts in one fortified barracks for the first time, enclosing roughly 440 by 380 meters whose masonry walls later became part of the Aurelian Walls. Its joint prefect in August 117, Publius Acilius Attianus, had been Hadrian's boyhood guardian and helped secure his succession the moment Trajan died.
properties.notes: Attianus served as joint praetorian prefect alongside Servius Sulpicius Similis at Trajan's death; Hadrian pushed Attianus into retirement in 119. The Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale now stands on part of the site, and stretches of the camp's north and east walls remain visible as part of the later Aurelian Walls.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 4.2
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Castra Praetoria
Historia Augusta, Hadrian 4, 9

properties.name: Castra Priora
properties.one_line: This camp housed the emperor's mounted bodyguard, the roughly 1,500-strong equites singulares Augusti, in a fort near the Lateran built under Domitian in the late first century. An 1885 excavation on Via Tasso uncovered its walls and inscribed pedestals naming the fort.
properties.notes: A larger second camp, the Castra Nova, was built close by only in 193 CE under Septimius Severus to house an enlarged 2,000-man guard, so it did not yet exist in 117 CE and is excluded from this map. The Castra Priora's exact perimeter has not been fully traced; this point follows the 1885 Via Tasso findspot.
sources: Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Castra Equitum Singularium
Wikipedia, Castra Nova equitum singularium

properties.name: Urban Cohorts Headquarters
properties.one_line: Rome's urban cohorts, the city's day-to-day police force created by Augustus as a counterweight to the Praetorian Guard, shared the Guard's fortified camp here rather than keeping a barracks of their own. They would not get a dedicated camp until Aurelian built the Castra Urbana more than 150 years later.
properties.notes: By 117 CE Rome most likely had four urban cohorts, numbered in continuation of the nine Praetorian cohorts (broadly X through XIII in the surviving epigraphic record), each about 500 men strong. Two further cohorts of the same series were permanently detached to Lugdunum and Carthage.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. cohortes urbanae
Cassius Dio, Roman History 55.24
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Castra (Urbana)

properties.name: Lugdunum Urban Cohort
properties.one_line: A single urban cohort, eventually numbered XIII, garrisoned Lugdunum for roughly two centuries to guard the city's imperial mint, one of the empire's most important.
properties.notes: Detached from Rome's urban cohort series under the Flavian emperors. No barracks building has been excavated; this point marks the Fourvière hill, the core of Roman Lugdunum, as a district-level approximation rather than a confirmed camp site.
sources: Musee Gallo-Romain de Lyon-Fourviere, epitaph of an optio of the cohors XIII urbana
Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. cohortes urbanae

properties.name: Carthage Urban Cohort
properties.one_line: Carthage hosted its own detached urban cohort, unusual for including mounted troops alongside infantry, the only such unit outside Rome and Lugdunum.
properties.notes: Detached from Rome's urban cohort series under the Flavian emperors, likely to help oversee the African grain fleet feeding Rome. No specific barracks site has been excavated; this point marks the Byrsa hill, the historic center of Roman Carthage, as a district-level approximation.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. cohortes urbanae
World History Encyclopedia, Cohortes Urbanae

properties.name: Ostia Urban Cohort
properties.one_line: Rome stationed a detachment of an urban cohort at its port city of Ostia to help protect the grain fleets that fed the capital.
properties.notes: Attested by inscriptions rather than an excavated barracks. This point marks the forum area of Ostia as a district-level approximation; the detachment's actual quarters have not been identified archaeologically.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. cohortes urbanae

properties.name: First Cohort of the Vigiles
properties.one_line: The First Cohort of Rome's fire brigade and night watch covered the Via Lata district near the Corso, with a guardhouse a seventeenth-century excavation found packed with statues honoring the unit's guardian spirit.
properties.notes: Located near Piazza dei Santi Apostoli based on a 1644 antiquarian report of vaulted halls with columns, mosaics, and statues of the Genius cohortis primae vigilum; no modern excavation has confirmed the guardhouse's exact footprint.
sources: Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: The Barracks in Rome
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stationes Vigilum

properties.name: Second Cohort of the Vigiles
properties.one_line: The Second Cohort's guardhouse stood in the area later occupied by the church of Santa Bibiana, near where Termini station now stands.
properties.notes: Location based on inscriptions found in the area rather than an excavated barracks building; treat this as a district-level approximation.
sources: Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: The Barracks in Rome
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stationes Vigilum

properties.name: Third Cohort of the Vigiles
properties.one_line: The Third Cohort watched over the Alta Semita district on the Quirinal, its guardhouse placed by scholars just south of where the Baths of Diocletian would later rise.
properties.notes: No excavated guardhouse has been identified; this point is a district-level approximation south of the later Baths of Diocletian, which were not built until the early fourth century.
sources: Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: The Barracks in Rome
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stationes Vigilum

properties.name: Fourth Cohort of the Vigiles
properties.one_line: The Fourth Cohort's guardhouse stood on the Aventine near where the church of San Saba now stands, its location fixed by inscriptions found in the area.
properties.notes: Inscriptions naming the cohort's Genius Centuriae were found around San Saba, giving a more confident district fix than most of the other cohorts, though no barracks structure itself has been excavated.
sources: Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: The Barracks in Rome
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stationes Vigilum

properties.name: Fifth Cohort of the Vigiles
properties.one_line: The Fifth Cohort's guardhouse stood on the Caelian Hill, and excavation beneath the later church of Santa Maria in Domnica uncovered part of its courtyard and portico.
properties.notes: Two inscriptions mentioning the Genius Centuriae were found below and beside the church, and partial excavation revealed a courtyard and porticus belonging to the guardhouse, giving this cohort one of the better-supported locations short of the excavated Trastevere excubitorium.
sources: Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: The Barracks in Rome
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stationes Vigilum

properties.name: Sixth Cohort of the Vigiles
properties.one_line: The Sixth Cohort covered the Forum district, its guardhouse placed by the ancient regionary catalogues near Trajan's Forum.
properties.notes: Location is a district-level approximation drawn from the regionary catalogues rather than an excavated building.
sources: Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: The Barracks in Rome
Platner & Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929), s.v. Stationes Vigilum

properties.name: Excubitorium of the Seventh Cohort
properties.one_line: This guardhouse for Trastevere's night watch and firefighters survives eight meters underground, complete with a hexagonal fountain, a black-and-white marine mosaic, and walls covered in graffiti the watchmen scratched during their shifts.
properties.notes: Discovered in 1865-66 beneath a private garden on what is now Via della Settima Coorte; it is the best-preserved and most precisely located vigiles guardhouse known, giving a hard anchor point missing for the other six cohorts.
sources: Turismo Roma, Excubitorium of the VII Cohort of the Vigiles
Ostia-Antica.org, Vigiles: A Guardhouse in Rome

properties.name: Pergamon
properties.one_line: This Greek city was the hometown of Gaius Julius Quadratus Bassus, a senator descended from the old Attalid and Galatian royal houses, who reached the consulship in 105 CE and was still commanding Trajan's armies in Dacia when he died there in 117.
properties.notes: One of the most prominent easterners in the Trajanic-Hadrianic senate; his career spanned governorships of Judea, Cappadocia-Galatia, Syria, and Dacia.
sources: Prosopographia Imperii Romani, I 507
Wikipedia, Gaius Julius Quadratus Bassus

properties.name: Espejo
properties.one_line: This small Baetican town was the hometown of Marcus Annius Verus, a senator who reached the consulship in 97 CE, served as Hadrian's prefect of the city, and raised his grandson, the future emperor Marcus Aurelius.
properties.notes: Ancient Ucubi, in Baetica near Corduba. Verus held a second consulship in 121 and a third in 126, cementing his family among the most influential Spanish-provincial houses in the Hadrianic senate.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Annius Verus, Marcus
Historia Augusta, Marcus Aurelius 1

properties.name: Faenza
properties.one_line: This northern Italian town was the birthplace of the senator Gaius Avidius Nigrinus, consul in 110 CE, who returned home only to be executed there in 118 as one of the four ex-consuls purged at the start of Hadrian's reign.
properties.notes: Ancient Faventia. Nigrinus was still a leading senator in good standing on 11 August 117; his fall came the following year, when the Senate had him and three other consulars killed on suspicion of plotting against Hadrian.
sources: Wikipedia, Gaius Avidius Nigrinus
Historia Augusta, Hadrian 7

properties.name: Marcus Appius Bradua, governor of Britannia
properties.one_line: A former consul of 108, Bradua has held Britain's frontier command for roughly two years and is still in post as news of Trajan's death crosses the empire — Hadrian replaces him within months.
properties.notes: Governed Britannia through a term modern scholarship brackets to roughly 115-118, putting him in office at the moment of the imperial transition even though no dated inscription pins him to 11 August 117 specifically.
sources: List of governors of Roman Britain (Wikipedia)
roman-britain.co.uk, s.v. Marcus Appius Bradua

properties.name: Lucius Tutilius Lupercus Pontianus, governor of Moesia Superior
properties.one_line: A senator who reached the suffect consulship around 105, Lupercus holds this Danube-frontier command opposite Dacia, the last governor of the province securely attested before a gap in the record until 120.
properties.notes: His governorship is attested only to around 115; nothing else is named until 120, so his presence specifically in 117 is inferred from that five-year gap rather than independently dated.
sources: List of Roman governors of Upper Moesia (Wikipedia)
Werner Eck, "Jahres- und Provinzialfasten der senatorischen Statthalter", Chiron 12 (1982)

properties.name: Gaius Julius Quadratus Bassus, governor of Dacia
properties.one_line: A veteran Trajanic general of Pergamene royal descent, Quadratus Bassus governs Trajan's newest conquest as frontier unrest flares right after the emperor's death — he dies in the province this same year putting it down.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Gaius Julius Quadratus Bassus
IGR IV 1302 (Pergamon cursus inscription)

properties.name: Quintus Pompeius Falco, governor of Moesia Inferior
properties.one_line: A trusted Trajanic general whose earlier commands ran through Lycia-Pamphylia and Judaea, Falco holds this Danube-mouth frontier as Hadrian takes power, before moving on within the year to command Britannia.
sources: List of Roman governors of Lower Moesia (Wikipedia)
CIL X 6321 (Tarracina cursus inscription)

properties.name: Aulus Platorius Nepos, governor of Thracia
properties.one_line: A rising favorite who will soon become one of Hadrian's closest confidants and later build Hadrian's Wall, Nepos governs Thracia as its praetorian legate in 117.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Aulus Platorius Nepos
Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Platorius Nepos, Aulus

properties.name: Lucius Catilius Severus, governor of Galatia et Cappadocia
properties.one_line: A close friend of Pliny the Younger and a decorated veteran of Trajan's Parthian campaign, Catilius Severus governs the combined Cappadocia-Armenia frontier command right as Trajan dies — within weeks Hadrian promotes him again, to succeed himself as legate of Syria.
properties.notes: His authority also extends over the freshly-conquered, jointly-administered territory of Armenia and Mesopotamia (its own entry in this project's province registry, folded here rather than given a second, speculatively-placed marker) — a command already unraveling as the Parthian revolt spreads, which Hadrian will formally abandon within months. No separate named legate is attested for the trans-Euphrates Mesopotamian territory as distinct from Cappadocia-Armenia.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Lucius Catilius Severus
CIL X 8291 = ILS 1041
Wikipedia, s.v. Mesopotamia (Roman province)

properties.name: Gaius Bruttius Praesens, governor of Cilicia
properties.one_line: A distinguished Trajanic general later tied by marriage into Marcus Aurelius's family, Praesens governs Cilicia as praetorian legate at the exact moment Trajan dies nearby at Selinus, putting him at the center of the succession.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Gaius Bruttius Praesens Lucius Fulvius Rusticus
List of Roman governors of Cilicia (Wikipedia)

properties.name: Publius Aelius Hadrianus, governor of Syria
properties.one_line: Trajan's second cousin and adopted heir commands Syria's legions as consular legate when news of Trajan's death reaches Antioch on 11 August 117 — that same army immediately hails him emperor, the exact event this map is frozen on.
properties.notes: His successor as legate of Syria, Lucius Catilius Severus, takes over only in October 117 when Hadrian departs for Rome — after this map's snapshot date, so not given his own marker here.
sources: Cass. Dio 69.1-2
HA Hadr. 4.6-4.7

properties.name: Lusius Quietus, governor of Iudaea
properties.one_line: A Berber prince turned Roman cavalry commander who broke Parthian siege lines for Trajan, Quietus holds Judaea as consular legate in the thick of the Kitos War — Hadrian strips him of the post within days of taking power and has him executed months later.
sources: Cass. Dio 68.32
Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 4.2.5

properties.name: Marcus Paccius Silvanus Quintus Coredius Gallus Gargilius Antiquus, governor of Arabia Petraea
properties.one_line: An African-born senator carrying one of the longest names in the Roman fasti, Gargilius Antiquus governs Arabia Petraea from Bostra through the Trajan-to-Hadrian transition, a tenure securely bracketed 116 to 119.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Quintus Coredius Gallus Gargilius Antiquus
List of Roman governors of Arabia Petraea (Wikipedia)

properties.name: Marcus Rutilius Lupus, prefect of Aegyptus
properties.one_line: Egypt's equestrian prefect since 113 — a senator could not hold this post by law — Lupus is on watch when the Kitos War erupts into open Jewish revolt across Alexandria and the countryside, a crisis so severe Trajan sends the praetorian prefect Marcius Turbo to help put it down.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Marcus Rutilius Lupus
Wikipedia, s.v. Praefectus Aegypti

properties.name: Gaius Julius Cornutus Tertullus, governor of Africa Proconsularis
properties.one_line: A veteran senator who once served as Pliny the Younger's colleague at the treasury and had earlier governed Bithynia-Pontus, Cornutus Tertullus caps his career as proconsul of Africa, the most senior senatorial governorship of all — and dies in office there in 117.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Gaius Julius Cornutus Tertullus
Journal of Roman Studies, "Cornutus Tertullus and the Plancii of Perge"

properties.name: Mainz
properties.one_line: The governor of Germania Superior ran his officium consularis from this Rhine fortress city, and the beneficiarii on his staff handled dispatches, tax oversight, and road security across the province.
properties.notes: Mogontiacum housed the governor of Germania Superior alongside the fortress of Legio XXII Primigenia, making it the natural seat of his officium consularis and its detachment of beneficiarii. A gravestone of a veteran and former beneficiarius consularis was recovered from the Roman cemetery street at Mainz-Weisenau, and other Mainz finds record men holding the related immunis consularis rank. Beneficiarii on a governor's staff served indefinitely rather than for a single term, giving Mogontiacum a standing administrative garrison distinct from the legion itself.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Mogontiacum
Archäologischer Anzeiger, "Eine neue Grabstele eines Veteranen und ehemaligen beneficiarius consularis aus Mainz-Weisenau"
R. Haensch, "Capita provinciarum" (officia of provincial governors)

properties.name: Bonn
properties.one_line: Bonna anchored the governor of Germania Inferior's military command, and beneficiarii drawn from the legion garrisoned here staffed his officium, policing the lower Rhine road and river crossing.
properties.notes: The legionary fortress at Bonna supplied beneficiarii to the governor of Germania Inferior's staff for as long as the province existed; a dedication catalogued as AE 1930, 26 records one such altar from the site. A later beneficiarius consularis inscription names the fortress's own garrison, Legio I Minervia, underlining how closely the officium's manpower was tied to whichever legion held Bonna. The bulk of surviving Bonna beneficiarii altars date from the later second and third centuries, so the practice at 117 CE is inferred from the standing garrison rather than a Trajanic-dated stone.
sources: R. Haensch, "Capita provinciarum" (officia of provincial governors)
Wikipedia, s.v. Bonna

properties.name: Eining
properties.one_line: Abusina guarded the point where the Danube frontier road met Raetia's inland route network, and beneficiarii lance-head insignia recovered here mark it as a staffed cursus publicus checkpoint.
properties.notes: Cohors IV Gallorum built Abusina's original earth-and-timber fort in 79-81 CE, well over a generation before this map's snapshot, at the spot where the Raetian limes road left the Danube for the interior. Excavators have recovered beneficiarius lance-head insignia from the Abusina-Eining site, physical proof of the rank's presence at what functioned as a road-security and customs checkpoint on the province's northern edge. Its position at a river-to-road junction made it exactly the kind of spot the officium consularis of Raetia would keep permanently staffed.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Abusina
ResearchGate, "Large and miniature spearshaped insignia of the Roman empire ('beneficiarius lances')"

properties.name: Petronell-Carnuntum
properties.one_line: The governor of Pannonia Superior ran his officium consularis from Carnuntum, and an altar to Jupiter Optimus Maximus still stands built into the site's ancient masonry.
properties.notes: Carnuntum served as the seat of the governor of Pannonia Superior as well as the fortress of Legio XIV Gemina, making the officium consularis and its beneficiarii detachment a standing feature of the site by the early second century. An altar dedicated to Jupiter Optimus Maximus, the deity beneficiarii overwhelmingly favored for their end-of-posting dedications, is set into the masonry near an entrance to the archaeological park today. As a full provincial capital rather than an outlying road station, Carnuntum's beneficiarii worked from inside the fortress and governor's residence itself rather than a separate rural shrine.
sources: Roamin' The Empire, "Carnuntum, Pannonia Superior"
R. Haensch, "Capita provinciarum" (officia of provincial governors)

properties.name: Ptuj
properties.one_line: Poetovio headquartered the portorium Illyrici, the customs office taxing goods along the entire Danube frontier, making it one of the empire's busiest beneficiarii and customs-police postings.
properties.notes: Poetovio grew from a legionary base into Colonia Ulpia Traiana Poetovio under Trajan and simultaneously served as the central administrative headquarters of the publicum portorium Illyrici, the customs district covering Noricum, both Pannonias, both Moesias, Dacia, and Thracia. The same freedman-procurator, Titus Iulius Capito, was honored for his portorium service in seven separate customs towns across this district, with Poetovio at its administrative core, and beneficiarii worked alongside the portorium's civilian slave and freedman staff to police the frontier's tax and road traffic. Few sites on the Danube combined a customs headquarters and a beneficiarii posting as thoroughly as Poetovio did in the early second century.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Poetovio
ostia-antica.org, "The district of the Publicum Portorii Illyrici"
researchgate.net, "Roman customs station from Capidava"

properties.name: Budapest
properties.one_line: Once Trajan split Pannonia in 107 CE, Aquincum became the governor's seat for Pannonia Inferior, and its officium consularis kept beneficiarii on hand to run the province's administration.
properties.notes: Aquincum anchored Pannonia Inferior as both the fortress of Legio II Adiutrix and, from the province's creation in 107 CE, the residence of its governor and his officium consularis. A governor's officium at a provincial capital always drew beneficiarii from the resident legion to staff his administrative, judicial, and courier needs, making their presence at Aquincum a structural certainty even where individual dedications are scarcer than at outlying road stations. The fortress was still under stone reconstruction when this map's snapshot falls, work begun essentially at the 117 CE date itself.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Aquincum
R. Haensch, "Capita provinciarum" (officia of provincial governors)

properties.name: Trebnje
properties.one_line: This station's very name, meaning the governor's post-house of the Latobici tribe, preserves its function as a fixed beneficiarii checkpoint on the road linking Italy to the Danube frontier.
properties.notes: Praetorium Latobicorum sat on the route linking Italy to the Danube, close to Celeia in the southwesternmost corner of Pannonia Superior, and multiple beneficiarii consulares dedications are known from the site. Its earliest securely dated altar carries a consular date of 158 CE, decades after this map's snapshot, and the station and its counterpart at Celeia are recorded alternating in use as the beneficiarii posting shifted between them over the second century. The road itself and the strategic need for a checkpoint here plausibly predate that first dated stone, but the specific station is documented with confidence only later, so this entry is flagged accordingly.
sources: Trismegistos, s.v. Praetorium Latobicorum (Trebnje)
Pleiades, s.v. Praetorium Latobicorum
R. L. Dise, "The beneficiarii procuratoris of Celeia and the development of the statio network"

properties.name: Sarmizegetusa
properties.one_line: Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa served as the governor's capital for Rome's newest province, and beneficiarii on his staff kept watch over Dacia's roads and dispatches from the moment the province was founded.
properties.notes: Founded by Trajan as Dacia's colonia and provincial capital after the conquest of 106 CE, Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa housed the governor and his officium consularis for the entire life of the new province. Beneficiarii consulares are documented across Roman Dacia's road network, and a governor's own capital was the administrative hub from which those postings were assigned and staffed. The province's officium is well studied through its epigraphic record, though the bulk of individually dated Dacian beneficiarii altars cluster in the decades after 117 CE rather than at the province's very founding.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa
academia.edu, "Officium consularis: The Evidence of Dacia"

properties.name: Alba Iulia
properties.one_line: Apulum's legionary fortress anchored Dacia's central road network, and beneficiarii drawn from its garrison, Legio XIII Gemina, staffed the province's cursus publicus and customs checkpoints.
properties.notes: Legio XIII Gemina moved to Apulum in 106 CE at Trajan's order to garrison the newly conquered province, and the fortress grew into Dacia's largest military and civilian settlement, sitting astride the road linking Sarmizegetusa to the province's northern frontier. Commanders and officers of the Thirteenth left a substantial epigraphic record at Apulum over the following century, including, by the Severan period, no fewer than seventeen dedicatory altars from the legion's commanders alone. Beneficiarii drawn from this same legion staffed the governor's officium and the surrounding road network from the province's earliest years.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Apulum (conurbation)
Wikipedia, s.v. Legio XIII Gemina

properties.name: Caseiu
properties.one_line: Samum's fort, raised the moment Trajan finished conquering Dacia, became one of the most thoroughly documented beneficiarii consularis postings on the province's northern frontier.
properties.notes: Trajan's army built Samum's timber fort in 101-102 CE, during the Dacian Wars themselves, on the road running north through what would become Dacia Porolissensis, and the site remained garrisoned for the next century and a half. Scholarship on Roman Dacia treats Samum as one of the province's best-documented beneficiarii consularis stations, with a large epigraphic assemblage of votive dedications recovered from its sacred precinct. Its founding date, squarely within Trajan's own reign, makes it one of the more securely Trajanic-era beneficiarii postings on this map rather than a station only attested generations later.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Samum (castrum)
academia.edu, "Les beneficiarii consularis de Samum"
academia.edu, "Religious Manifestations of beneficiarii consularis of Roman Dacia"

properties.name: Kostolac
properties.one_line: Viminacium anchored Moesia Superior's governor and the fleet base watching the Danube, and its officium consularis staffed beneficiarii to run the province's roads and river traffic.
properties.notes: Viminacium served as the seat of the governor of Moesia Superior and the fortress of Legio VII Claudia, combining military, administrative, and river-fleet functions at a single bend of the Danube. A governor's capital of this scale required a standing officium consularis, and beneficiarii drawn from the resident legion were its natural enforcement arm for road security and customs oversight along this stretch of frontier. The city later grew into one of the largest urban centers on the Danube, with a population estimated at up to 40,000 at its height.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Viminacium
R. Haensch, "Capita provinciarum" (officia of provincial governors)

properties.name: Lyon
properties.one_line: The governor of Gallia Lugdunensis ran his officium from Lugdunum, and a beneficiarius on his staff is named on a securely dated first-century career inscription from the city.
properties.notes: Lugdunum was the provincial capital of Gallia Lugdunensis and home to its governor's officium consularis for the entire life of the province. A career inscription records a soldier of the cohors I urbana, Lugdunum's own garrison unit, serving as beneficiarius to the governor Tettienus Serenus starting around 79 CE before being promoted to cornicularius under his successors in 83, giving Gaul's beneficiarii network a securely first-century anchor point. Because Lugdunum's beneficiarii worked from inside the governor's own residence rather than a separate rural shrine, no dedicated votive precinct comparable to the Rhine and Danube frontier sanctuaries has been identified in the city.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. cohortes urbanae
Virginia Tech Scholarly Communication, "ElAnt v4n1 - Beneficiarius Eius"

properties.name: Geneva
properties.one_line: A beneficiarii detachment guarded Genava's Rhone bridge and staffed its customs post, collecting the quadragesima Galliarum, the 2.5 percent toll levied on goods crossing into and out of Gaul.
properties.notes: Genava sat at the edge of the Swiss plateau where the roads from Italy and Narbonensis converged on the Rhone, and its river traffic and two harbors made it a natural collection point for the quadragesima Galliarum, the empire's Gallic customs tax. A military post staffed by beneficiarii guarded the Rhone bridge here specifically to secure this toll station, one of the clearest documented cases anywhere of beneficiarii doing customs-police duty exactly as this category describes. Though legally only a vicus within the civitas of Vienna, Genava's commercial and administrative weight far outstripped its formal status.
sources: Roamin' The Empire, "Genava, Gallia Narbonensis"
Grokipedia, "Quadragesima Galliarum"
Perseus, Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, s.v. Genava

properties.name: Tarragona
properties.one_line: This city was the hometown of Lucius Licinius Sura, Trajan's closest confidant, who held an exceptional three consulships and advised the emperor through the Dacian Wars.
properties.notes: Sura's third consulship, in 107 CE, was a mark of favor almost unheard of outside the imperial family itself. Martial and Pliny the Younger both counted him as a personal friend, and Cassius Dio credited him with unmatched influence over Trajan.
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 68.15
Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Licinius Sura, Lucius
Pliny, Epistulae 4.30, 7.27

properties.name: Como
properties.one_line: This town was the hometown of Pliny the Younger, consul in 100 CE and later Trajan's special legate to Bithynia-Pontus, who called it 'my own Comum' in his letters.
properties.notes: An inscription originally set over the baths Pliny funded at Comum, later reused in Milan's Sant'Ambrogio, records his full career and the roughly 1.87 million sesterces he left the city for civic benefactions.
sources: Pliny, Epistulae 1.8, 4.13
CIL V 5262
Pliny, Panegyricus (delivered on his consulship, 100 CE)

properties.name: Sepino
properties.one_line: This Samnite town was the hometown of Lucius Neratius Priscus, head of the Proculian school of law, suffect consul in 97 CE, and a jurist on Hadrian's advisory council.
properties.notes: Priscus governed Germania Inferior and Pannonia and sat on Hadrian's council into the 130s. His juristic writings, the Regulae and Membrana, survive only in excerpts quoted by the later Digest.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Neratius Priscus, Lucius
Wikipedia, s.v. Lucius Neratius Priscus

properties.name: Sepino
properties.one_line: This Samnite town also produced Lucius Neratius Marcellus, brother of the jurist Priscus, who governed Roman Britain as Trajan's consular legate around 103 CE.
properties.notes: A military discharge diploma found near Caerleon dates Marcellus's tenure as governor of Britain precisely to 19 January 103. His childless uncle, Marcus Hirrius Fronto Neratius Pansa, had adopted him.
sources: roman-britain.co.uk, s.v. Lucius Neratius Marcellus
Roman military discharge diploma, Caerleon, dated 19 January 103

properties.name: Bolsena
properties.one_line: This town was the hometown of Aulus Cornelius Palma Frontonianus, who reached a second consulship in 109 CE as Trajan's reward for annexing Nabataea as the province of Arabia.
properties.notes: Palma also governed Hispania Tarraconensis and Syria. Hadrian, wary of his standing, had him executed in 118 as one of four ex-consuls purged at the start of the new reign.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Cornelius Palma Frontonianus, Aulus
Historia Augusta, Hadrian 7

properties.name: Antalya
properties.one_line: This Pamphylian city is the disputed hometown of Gaius Julius Cornutus Tertullus, suffect consul in 100 CE alongside Pliny the Younger, who died in office governing Africa in 117.
properties.notes: The Oxford Classical Dictionary places Cornutus Tertullus at Attaleia, while Ronald Syme argued from his career inscription's dedicator that he actually came from neighboring Perge instead. Both are real, specific, competing identifications, not a vague guess.
sources: Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Iulius Cornutus Tertullus, Gaius
Journal of Roman Studies, "Cornutus Tertullus and the Plancii of Perge"

properties.name: Faenza
properties.one_line: This town also produced Titus Avidius Quietus, suffect consul in 93 CE and governor of Britain under Trajan, father of the already-mapped consul Gaius Avidius Nigrinus.
properties.notes: Quietus was an intimate friend of the Stoic martyr Thrasea Paetus and later of Plutarch, who dedicated a treatise to him. He governed Britain roughly 98 to 101 CE.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Titus Avidius Quietus
List of governors of Roman Britain (Wikipedia)

properties.name: Buccino
properties.one_line: This Lucanian town was the hometown of Gaius Bruttius Praesens, the first of his family to reach the consulship, who commanded a legion in Trajan's Parthian War.
properties.notes: Praesens commanded Legio VI Ferrata during Trajan's Parthian campaign of 114-115 and was governing Cilicia when Trajan died at nearby Selinus in August 117. Pliny the Younger addressed him directly as a Lucanian.
sources: Pliny, Epistulae 7.3
Wikipedia, s.v. Gaius Bruttius Praesens Lucius Fulvius Rusticus

properties.name: Barcelona
properties.one_line: This city was the hometown of Lucius Minicius Natalis, who governed Numidia and reached the suffect consulship in 106 CE after winning decorations in Trajan's Dacian Wars.
properties.notes: An honorific monument to Natalis's son, set up in Barcino by the colonia of Carthage, identifies the city as the family's hometown, where Natalis later served as civic patron.
sources: Werner Eck, "Das Ehrenmonument der Colonia Carthago fur L. Minicius Natalis Quadronius Verus in seiner Heimatstadt Barcino"
Wikipedia, s.v. Lucius Minicius Natalis

properties.name: Santiponce
properties.one_line: This Baetican colony was the hometown of Trajan himself, who reached the suffect consulship in 91 CE and governed Germania Superior before his acclamation as emperor in 98.
properties.notes: Trajan's own father, also named Marcus Ulpius Traianus, had likewise reached the consulship and governed Syria from the same hometown a generation earlier.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 13.1
Cassius Dio, Roman History 68.4
Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Trajan

properties.name: Santiponce
properties.one_line: This same colony is the disputed birthplace of Hadrian, who reached the suffect consulship in 108 CE and held the legateship of Syria when Trajan died in August 117.
properties.notes: The Historia Augusta states Hadrian was born in Rome, yet the same source also quotes his own autobiography claiming Italica, his father's hometown, instead. Most modern scholarship favors Italica.
sources: Historia Augusta, Hadrian 1.3
Wikipedia, s.v. Hadrian

properties.name: Mudanya
properties.one_line: This Bithynian city is the scholarly-inferred hometown of Lucius Catilius Severus, who commanded Trajan's Cappadocian frontier and became consul again in 120 alongside the future emperor Antoninus Pius.
properties.notes: Catilius Severus reached his first suffect consulship in 110 CE. Hadrian promoted him within weeks of Trajan's death to succeed himself as legate of Syria. The Bithynian origin rests on inference from his names rather than a direct inscription, so it is marked accordingly.
sources: Wikipedia, s.v. Lucius Catilius Severus
R. Syme, discussion of Catilius Severus's Bithynian origins in scholarship on the career of Arrian
